stories.headline: Assam: The Great Khali extends support to flood-affected people in Nazira
stories.title: Assam: The Great Khali extends support to flood-affected people in Nazira
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: NAZIRA: Internationally acclaimed WWE champion and Indian professional wrestler Dalip Singh Rana, popularly known as ‘The Great Khali,’ has reached out to flood-affected people in Assam during his two-day visit to Sivasagar district.
After participating in a relief-material distribution programme at Dorika Kaibarta village in Sivasagar on Thursday, Khali visited Chumani village in Nazira on Friday.

The programme was organised by True Hope Foundation, Ayan and Deeplina Deka Foundation, which distributed essential items including beds, mattresses, fans, and water filters among flood-affected families.
Khali subsequently visited Tengahola at Bamun Pukhuri, where he participated in an ongoing house-construction initiative undertaken by the three organisations for flood victims.
He inaugurated one newly constructed house at the site.
He also laid the foundation stone for a proposed Hanuman temple to be constructed in the same area under the initiative of True Hope Foundation, Ayan and Deeplina Deka Foundation.

Appreciating the organisations and volunteers involved in rebuilding homes for flood-affected families, Khali said, “Best wishes for this initiative to construct more than 100 houses for flood victims.
May God give greater strength to all the volunteers and organisers so that they can continue serving many more people in society.”
Khali’s visit and participation in the relief and rehabilitation initiatives brought encouragement to the flood-affected families and volunteers engaged in the ongoing reconstruction efforts.

stories.headline: Assam citizens’ forum calls for scientific solution to flood problem
stories.title: Assam citizens’ forum calls for scientific solution to flood problem
stories.summary: The CPI(M) organises ‘demand day’ to seek the national disaster tag for the State’s annual deluge
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A citizens’ forum in Assam has called for a comprehensive and scientific approach to the flood problem—one that looks beyond temporary relief and embankment repairs and examines the entire river and ecological system.

On Friday (August 21, 2026), members of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) organised ‘demand day’, seeking the national disaster tag for the deluge that leaves scores dead and displaces thousands every year.
The party also demanded ₹20 lakh for the families of those killed in the recent floods, ₹1 lakh in immediate assistance to each affected family and up to ₹10 lakh for houses destroyed in the floods.

The Assam Nagorik Sammilan, a forum headed by academician Hiren Gohain and former Director General of Police Harekrishna Deka, said the State’s geographical position makes it vulnerable to flooding via rivers originating in the mountains of the surrounding hill States.
“It is therefore only natural that construction, mining and other large-scale activities in the upper reaches of these river systems will affect the volume and speed of water flowing into Assam.
And that is precisely where we are witnessing serious changes,” the forum said, citing the recent devastation in Sivasagar, Charaideo, and Jorhat districts.
The forum also warned of a similar disaster if the Eco-Sensitive Zone around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve is reduced to 1 k.m. from the default 10 km.
“Kaziranga’s Eco-Sensitive Zone cannot be treated as an issue separate from the larger environmental crisis facing Assam.
The conservation of forests, wetlands, and floodplains is closely connected to the State’s ecological security and its ability to cope with floods,” it said.

The forum announced a plan for a convention to bring together environmentalists, forest experts, engineers, river specialists, geologists, historians, social scientists, activists, and people from flood-affected areas to examine the flood and environmental crisis from every possible perspective.

The perspectives include the impact of climate change, changes in river systems, embankments, dams and other infrastructure, mining, deforestation, wetlands, floodplains and the larger development model being followed in the northeast.

stories.headline: Trump loyalist Ed Martin leaves DOJ to focus on election legal battles
stories.title: Trump loyalist Ed Martin leaves DOJ to focus on election legal battles
stories.summary: Ed Martin, a loyal White House ally who held multiple Justice Department posts despite unconventional tactics that sometimes rankled his superiors, is leaving President Donald Trump's administration, the Republican president said Friday. Trump said in a social media post that Martin is leaving his role as the Justice Department's pardon attorney to "fight Legal Battles" surrounding this year's midterm elections and the 2028 presidential election. "I know he will do an outstanding job, ensure Free, Fair, and Honest Elections, and strongly advance our Constitutional Rights," Trump wrote. Martin has been a controversial Trump administration figure since his appointment last year as interim US attorney for the District of Columbia, where he oversaw the dismissal of Jan. 6 cases after Trump's sweeping pardons. Trump later pulled Martin's nomination for the job over bipartisan concerns about his lack of prosecutorial experience and support for rioters who violently attacked the Capitol.

stories.headline: Kashmiriyat in Stone and Deodar
stories.title: Kashmiriyat in Stone and Deodar
stories.summary: The preservation and thoughtful integration of Kashmir’s unique architectural, religious, and historical sites into sustainable eco-tourism hubs is essential for safeguarding the valley’s syncretic cultural ethos. Unlike standard Islamic architecture across the world, Kashmir’s traditional Islamic structures—such as the Khanqah-e-Moula and Jama Masjid—showcase a distinct Vernacular Wooden Architecture, defined by tiered pyramidal roofs (Shikhara-style roofs), heavy deodar woodwork, and intricate papier-mache or Pinjrakari (lattice work). This reflects a seamless fusion of indigenous Kashmiri Buddhist-Hindu stone craftsmanship with Central Asian Sufi motifs. Likewise, early Kashmiri Hindu temples—from the 8th-century Awantipora and Parihaspura ruins and Nara Nag complex to Shankaracharya—utilize grand stone masonry with distinct triangular gables, trefoil arches, and cella-in-water layouts (Kunds), representing a distinct school of ancient architecture unparalleled in continental India. Priority Heritage Sites & Adaptive Tourism Development Khanqah-e-Moula & Shahr-e-Khas (Downtown) are the premier examples of Kashmiri wooden pagoda-style architecture dedicated to Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani; epicentre of central valley craft culture. Development of heritage walk circuits and restoration of the traditional Zoon Dub (overhanging balconies) and brick facades along the Jhelum riverfront. Integrating river transit (Shikara routes) with guided walking tours will be very much appreciated by everybody including the tourists. Likewise, the Awantipora Ruins, Parihaspura & Naranag Temple Complex are the 8th to 9th-century Utpala and Karkota dynasty stone temples showing distinctive Kashmiri classical architecture of the periods of King Lalitaditya Muktapida. These need to have a restorative look and signages and short movies describing the historic times of the past surrounded by pleasant parks and gardens with an entry fee if found feasible. Hari Parbat Belt (Sharika Temple, Makhdoom Sahib, Gurdwara Chatti Padshahi) The multi-faith hill shrine showcasing Kashmiriyat and Kashmir’s shared spiritual history. Creating continuous pedestrian greenways, herbal gardens, terraced viewpoints, and eco-friendly battery vehicle transportation across the hill complex will be a great teaching history lessons of our mixed culture. These of course will be good revenue earners for the dept. of tourism besides showcasing these historical venues. Rishi Peer (Ali Kadal) is a deeply revered local shrine, and a Rishi-Sufi habitats that represent community-level heritage revered by both Pandits and Muslims. Over the years it seems to have lost its importance with the mass exodus of Pandits. Such places are good examples for Community Restoration. It needs implementation of localized conservation using traditional materials (lime mortar, local stone) paired with neighbourhood green spaces and heritage signage. Ishber and Nishat Belt (Swami Lakshman Joo Ashram & Jeethyar) are centres of Kashmir Shaivism and ancient holy springs (Nagasha) and Goddess Jyshta located along the Dal foothills. These are ideal spots for meditation and developing eco-gardens to preserve the serene environment with quiet reflection zones, native floral landscaping, and digital archives of Kashmiri Shaiva philosophy. Perched atop the adjacent Gopadri Hill on the Zabarwan range, the Shankaracharya Temple stands as a timeless spiritual and historical anchor overlooking Srinagar. Dedicated to Lord Shiva, the stone structure dates back to antiquity, with local traditions attributing its earliest foundations to Jaluka, son of Emperor Ashoka, before being reconstructed by later rulers. The site earned its iconic name after the philosopher Adi Shankaracharya visited Kashmir in the 8th century AD to engage in philosophical debates, meditating at this very spot to revive Advaita Vedanta. Reaching the shrine requires ascending 243 stone steps, rewarding pilgrims and visitors with sweeping panoramic views of Dal Lake and the Jhelum valley—serving as a symbolic precursor to the cultural and scientific intellectualism that later flourished just down the ridge at Pari Mahal. This area needs to build a scenic cable car connecting the Boulevard Road/Dal Lake base to Chashme Shahi, Pari Mahal, and the Shankaracharya foothills to reduce traffic choke points along the winding hill road. An eco-Friendly Shuttle fleet by deploying electric mini-buses to manage hill transport and reduce carbon emissions in the fragile Zabarwan ecosystem. Beyond the manicured terraces of Chashme Shahi, Pari Mahal (the Palace of Fairies) and the associated library ruins of Prince Dara Shikoh represent a pivotal era of Mughal Kashmir, where architectural grandiosity converged with intellectual syncretism. Perched dramatically above Dal Lake, Pari Mahal was constructed in the mid-17th century by Dara Shikoh—the scholar-prince and eldest son of Shah Jahan—not merely as a pleasure garden, but as an observatory, a retreat for Sufi contemplation, and a vibrant centre for the study of astronomy and astrology under his spiritual mentor, Mullah Shah Badakhshi. The site housed a vast library containing priceless manuscripts on comparative religion, Persian translations of the Upanishads (Sirr-i-Akbar), and scientific treatises. Beyond its historic intellectual legacy, Pari Mahal’s heritage value lies in its unique terraced stone architecture, which departs from classic Mughal brick-and-plaster construction in favour of local grey granite masonry adorned with vaulted arches, subterranean chambers, and intricate water channels. Restoring these partially ruined terraces and intellectual halls through rigorous conservation—utilizing lime mortar, localized stone dressing, and timber retrofitting—is crucial for resurrecting their historical identity. To help visitors truly realize the forgotten grandeur of this sanctuary, the site requires context-rich interpretative signages, tactile 3D models of the original six-tiered structure, and QR-enabled digital displays mapping the cosmic and literary pursuits of Dara Shikoh, transforming these evocative ruins into a living centre of Kashmir’s scholastic past. To restore and preserve these invaluable places we need to enforce precise material codes for restoration—prohibiting modern concrete/aluminium cladding in heritage zones like Shahr-e-Khas. Promote traditional earthquake-resistant structural practices such as Dhajji Dewari (timber frame with brick infill) and Taq (timber-laced masonry). By preventing illegal encroachment around historic monuments through marked green belts and strict zoning laws. What we need is craft & culture integration by linking spiritual circuits with local artisanal neighbourhoods (Kani shawl weavers, Papier-mâché experts, copper-smiths, wood carvers), ensuring tourism directly benefits local communities and preserves traditional livelihoods. Providing curated signage, QR-coded audio guides, and localized heritage centres at major hubs to educate visitors on the multi-layered history of the Kashmir valley. Ultimately, the future of Kashmir’s tourism lies not in rapid modernization, but in the meticulous preservation of its physical and spiritual history. By enforcing traditional material codes, protecting the architectural brilliance of both stone and timber, and directly empowering local artisans, the valley can build a sustainable model of eco-tourism. Transforming these priority sites into living heritage hubs does more than secure a steady revenue stream or reduce environmental impact; it revives the fading links of community restoration. Protecting this landscape ensures that the physical remnants of the past—from the grand terraces of Pari Mahal to the quiet sanctuaries of the Sufi-Rishi shrines—continue to stand as a testament to Kashmiriyat, safeguarding the valley’s unique, syncretic cultural ethos for generations to come. Prof Upendra Kaul, Founder Director Gauri Kaul Foundation

stories.headline: Gor in Kashmir: The Signal Behind the Soundbite
stories.title: Gor in Kashmir: The Signal Behind the Soundbite
stories.summary: Sergio Gor’s first visit to Kashmir as the U.S. Ambassador to India was not just another diplomatic stop on a crowded calendar of official engagements. It was a carefully weighted political act, one that carried meaning far beyond the polite language of courtesy, development, and security. When a senior American envoy stands in Srinagar and describes Jammu and Kashmir as an “important part of India,” the statement is not merely descriptive. It is a signal, and in the present geopolitical moment, signals matter almost as much as policy itself. Washington has long preferred ambiguity on Kashmir. That ambiguity was useful because it allowed the United States to preserve working relations with India without entirely foreclosing its channels with Pakistan. But ambiguity has costs. It can sound like caution, yet it often appears to the parties on the ground as evasiveness, and to Pakistan as a diplomatic cover under which it continues to press its old claims. Gor’s remarks suggest that the balance may be shifting, at least in tone if not yet in formal doctrine. In diplomacy, tone often comes before text. The timing of the visit adds another layer. This was not a random tourism trip or a ceremonial photo opportunity. Gor arrived in a Kashmir that has been at the center of regional politics, international commentary, and domestic contestation for decades. He met the political leadership, spoke in a language that clearly pleased New Delhi and irritated Islamabad, and hinted that Washington may review its travel advisory for the region. That last point is especially significant. If the advisory is downgraded, it would mark more than a bureaucratic adjustment. It would amount to a powerful symbolic vote of confidence in the ground situation, suggesting that the U.S. sees Kashmir less as a frozen conflict zone and more as a space where normalcy, commerce, and controlled political life are increasingly visible. This is precisely why Pakistan reacted with such anger. Islamabad’s diplomatic posture on Kashmir depends on one central assumption: that the world must continue to treat the territory as a disputed question in motion, never as a settled part of India. So when a top U.S. envoy uses language that aligns more closely with India’s constitutional and political position, it cuts into Pakistan’s preferred narrative. The demarche was therefore predictable. But its predictability does not weaken its significance. It reveals the fragility of Pakistan’s diplomatic leverage at a time when its stock in Washington is no longer what it once was. For years, Pakistan relied on strategic utility. It was courted as a counterweight in Afghanistan, a logistical partner in regional crises, and a state whose cooperation could not be ignored. That era is over, or at least seriously diminished. In the current phase, Pakistan brings fewer advantages to the table, while India offers a much larger strategic, economic, technological, and symbolic return. The American political establishment may still speak the language of balance, but the underlying instinct is unmistakably shifting toward India. Gor’s statement on Kashmir should be seen in that context. There is also the Trump factor. Donald Trump’s foreign policy style has always been transactional, theatrical, and impatient with long diplomatic scripts. He likes visible wins, striking language, and gestures that project force without necessarily entangling him in permanent commitments. At a time when his administration faces criticism and resistance over Iran, Ukraine, and wider global pushback, a firmer, more visible pro-India stance offers several advantages. It helps him appear decisive in South Asia without having to pay the heavy costs of direct confrontation elsewhere. It gives him a narrative of geopolitical momentum. And it allows him to frame India as a rising partner in an American-led order that is being recalibrated, not abandoned. That recalibration becomes clearer when one looks beyond Kashmir and toward the broader ideological ecosystem in which India’s ruling and quasi-ruling nationalist currents operate. The RSS’s overseas outreach, especially the visits and public engagements of its top leaders in the United States, reflects a conscious effort to internationalize its message and normalize its worldview in influential diaspora and policy circles. This does not mean the RSS is directing U.S. policy. It does mean that Indian nationalist actors have become increasingly skilled at shaping the language through which India is discussed abroad. They are no longer confined to domestic politics. They are participating in the global production of legitimacy. That matters because the Kashmir question is not only about territory. It is also about narrative power. Who gets to define what Kashmir is? A disputed land? A security challenge? A post-Article 370 constitutional reality? A place of conflict? A place of recovery? A place of investment? A place of civic life? Every external statement nudges the answer in one direction or another. Gor’s choice of words nudges it toward India’s sovereignty claim and toward the idea that Kashmir is stabilizing sufficiently to warrant a different international posture. For Kashmiris, however, the issue is more complex. There is understandable appeal in any development that might reduce stigma, improve connectivity, encourage tourism, and make the region less vulnerable to being framed solely through conflict. A lower travel advisory may help business, people-to-people contact, and international confidence. But Kashmiris also know that symbolic validation from outside powers does not automatically translate into deeper political justice, institutional trust, or democratic resolution. International reassurance can coexist with local unresolvedness. A foreign envoy’s positive statement can never replace the hard questions of representation, rights, accountability, and political agency. That is why one should resist the temptation to read Gor’s visit as either a breakthrough or a betrayal. It is neither. It is a calibrated diplomatic move in a shifting strategic environment. It reflects a U.S. desire to speak more directly to India’s core position, to irritate Pakistan at low cost, and to align with the broader American instinct to invest in India as a long-term strategic partner. It also reflects a larger truth: Kashmir remains central not because the region itself has changed into a global stage by choice, but because major powers continue to treat it as one. The deeper question is what happens if this pattern persists. If Washington continues to soften its caution, if it increasingly echoes Indian language, if Pakistan’s protests become routine background noise, and if diaspora politics and ideological outreach deepen the alignment, then the Kashmir discourse will undergo an important shift. The region will be discussed less as an unresolved international problem and more as a normalizing domestic space whose external image is being repaired. That may help India’s diplomatic goals. It may please those who want a cleaner global narrative. But it will also sharpen the challenge for Kashmiris to ensure that normalization does not become a substitute for genuine political listening. There is, finally, a warning in all of this. The RSS may be more visible abroad; it does not control the American state. And Kashmir may be receiving warmer words; it still bears the burden of its unresolved history. The soundbite was short. The signal is much larger as Mirza Ghalib would have us believe “Bekhudi besabab Nahin Ghalib | Kuch to hai jis ki parda dari hai!!”. opening: Sergio Gor’s first visit to Kashmir as the U.S. Ambassador to India was not just another diplomatic stop on a crowded calendar of official engagements.
It was a carefully weighted political act, one that carried meaning far beyond the polite language of courtesy, development, and security.
body: When a senior American envoy stands in Srinagar and describes Jammu and Kashmir as an “important part of India,” the statement is not merely descriptive.
It is a signal, and in the present geopolitical moment, signals matter almost as much as policy itself.
Washington has long preferred ambiguity on Kashmir.
That ambiguity was useful because it allowed the United States to preserve working relations with India without entirely foreclosing its channels with Pakistan.
But ambiguity has costs.
Gor’s remarks suggest that the balance may be shifting, at least in tone if not yet in formal doctrine.
In diplomacy, tone often comes before text.
The timing of the visit adds another layer.
This was not a random tourism trip or a ceremonial photo opportunity.
Gor arrived in a Kashmir that has been at the center of regional politics, international commentary, and domestic contestation for decades.
He met the political leadership, spoke in a language that clearly pleased New Delhi and irritated Islamabad, and hinted that Washington may review its travel advisory for the region.
That last point is especially significant.
If the advisory is downgraded, it would mark more than a bureaucratic adjustment.

It would amount to a powerful symbolic vote of confidence in the ground situation, suggesting that the U.S. sees Kashmir less as a frozen conflict zone and more as a space where normalcy, commerce, and controlled political life are increasingly visible.
This is precisely why Pakistan reacted with such anger.
Islamabad’s diplomatic posture on Kashmir depends on one central assumption: that the world must continue to treat the territory as a disputed question in motion, never as a settled part of India.
So when a top U.S. envoy uses language that aligns more closely with India’s constitutional and political position, it cuts into Pakistan’s preferred narrative.
The demarche was therefore predictable.
But its predictability does not weaken its significance.
It reveals the fragility of Pakistan’s diplomatic leverage at a time when its stock in Washington is no longer what it once was.
For years, Pakistan relied on strategic utility.
It was courted as a counterweight in Afghanistan, a logistical partner in regional crises, and a state whose cooperation could not be ignored.
That era is over, or at least seriously diminished.
In the current phase, Pakistan brings fewer advantages to the table, while India offers a much larger strategic, economic, technological, and symbolic return.
The American political establishment may still speak the language of balance, but the underlying instinct is unmistakably shifting toward India.
Gor’s statement on Kashmir should be seen in that context.
There is also the Trump factor.
Donald Trump’s foreign policy style has always been transactional, theatrical, and impatient with long diplomatic scripts.
He likes visible wins, striking language, and gestures that project force without necessarily entangling him in permanent commitments.
At a time when his administration faces criticism and resistance over Iran, Ukraine, and wider global pushback, a firmer, more visible pro-India stance offers several advantages.
It helps him appear decisive in South Asia without having to pay the heavy costs of direct confrontation elsewhere.
It gives him a narrative of geopolitical momentum.
And it allows him to frame India as a rising partner in an American-led order that is being recalibrated, not abandoned.
That recalibration becomes clearer when one looks beyond Kashmir and toward the broader ideological ecosystem in which India’s ruling and quasi-ruling nationalist currents operate.

The RSS’s overseas outreach, especially the visits and public engagements of its top leaders in the United States, reflects a conscious effort to internationalize its message and normalize its worldview in influential diaspora and policy circles.
This does not mean the RSS is directing U.S. policy.
It does mean that Indian nationalist actors have become increasingly skilled at shaping the language through which India is discussed abroad.
They are no longer confined to domestic politics.
They are participating in the global production of legitimacy.
That matters because the Kashmir question is not only about territory.
It is also about narrative power.
Who gets to define what Kashmir is?
A disputed land?
A security challenge?
A post-Article 370 constitutional reality?
A place of conflict?
A place of recovery?
A place of investment?
A place of civic life?
Every external statement nudges the answer in one direction or another.
Gor’s choice of words nudges it toward India’s sovereignty claim and toward the idea that Kashmir is stabilizing sufficiently to warrant a different international posture.
For Kashmiris, however, the issue is more complex.
There is understandable appeal in any development that might reduce stigma, improve connectivity, encourage tourism, and make the region less vulnerable to being framed solely through conflict.
A lower travel advisory may help business, people-to-people contact, and international confidence.
But Kashmiris also know that symbolic validation from outside powers does not automatically translate into deeper political justice, institutional trust, or democratic resolution.
International reassurance can coexist with local unresolvedness.
A foreign envoy’s positive statement can never replace the hard questions of representation, rights, accountability, and political agency.
That is why one should resist the temptation to read Gor’s visit as either a breakthrough or a betrayal.
It is neither.
It is a calibrated diplomatic move in a shifting strategic environment.

It reflects a U.S. desire to speak more directly to India’s core position, to irritate Pakistan at low cost, and to align with the broader American instinct to invest in India as a long-term strategic partner.
It also reflects a larger truth: Kashmir remains central not because the region itself has changed into a global stage by choice, but because major powers continue to treat it as one.
The deeper question is what happens if this pattern persists.

If Washington continues to soften its caution, if it increasingly echoes Indian language, if Pakistan’s protests become routine background noise, and if diaspora politics and ideological outreach deepen the alignment, then the Kashmir discourse will undergo an important shift.
The region will be discussed less as an unresolved international problem and more as a normalizing domestic space whose external image is being repaired.
That may help India’s diplomatic goals.
It may please those who want a cleaner global narrative.
But it will also sharpen the challenge for Kashmiris to ensure that normalization does not become a substitute for genuine political listening.

stories.headline: "Abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism...": Iran slams latest slew of US sanctions
stories.title: "Abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism...": Iran slams latest slew of US sanctions
stories.summary: Tehran , August 22 : Iran on Saturday slammed the latest economic sanctions announced by the United States, calling them arbitrary and saying they have no basis in international law and violate the principle of sovereign equality enshrined in the UN Charter. The remarks were made by Esmaeil Baqaei, spokesperson for Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in a post on X on Saturday. "The United States' declaration of new economic sanctions on Iran is far more than continued unlawful 'economic warfare' against a single country. It is an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent Member State of the United Nations," Baqaei said. He said no country can lawfully compel foreign banks, enterprises or airports, which are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of their respective sovereign states, to halt lawful commerce with a third country. "Such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law. They violate the principle of sovereign equality enshrined in Article 2(1) of the UN Charter and breach the customary prohibition on intervention affirmed by the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case," he said. Baqaei further alleged that economic coercion aimed at forcing a sovereign state to alter its lawful policy choices amounts to an internationally wrongful act. "When combined with a naval blockade amounting to military aggression, these demands reduce the sovereignty of all other States to something provisional, conditional, and revocable at the whim of another power," he said. He added that compliance with such sanctions does not guarantee immunity or respect, but instead means accepting that banks, enterprises and airports operate "only under a foreign licence." "The end result would be the complete erosion of sovereignty as the foundational basis of the UN-based inter-State system, and a recipe for an abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism," Baqaei said. His remarks come after Washington announced a fresh round of sanctions targeting Iran, amid continued tensions between the two countries and broader instability in West Asia. Trump recently announced what he called the "most crushing economic operation ever taken" against Iran and warned countries providing financial, business or government support to Tehran of "tremendous economic consequences". The US President said the measures would target Iran's economic lifelines, including oil smuggling networks, financial transfers, exchange houses, ship registries and front companies. He also called the campaign an "Economic D-Day" and urged American allies to join Washington in isolating Iran. (ANI)

stories.headline: BRICS+ Legal Forum Delegates Visit Supreme Court, Hold Bilateral Consultations Before Inauguration
stories.title: BRICS+ Legal Forum Delegates Visit Supreme Court, Hold Bilateral Consultations Before Inauguration
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Senior legal delegations participating in the 11th BRICS+ Legal Forum held bilateral meetings at the India Habitat Centre in New Delhi on Friday, ahead of the formal inauguration of the Forum on August 22.

The bilateral consultations, hosted by the Bar Association of India (BAI), brought together representatives of participating BRICS+ jurisdictions for discussions on strengthening cooperation among legal institutions, bar associations and the wider legal profession.
The Indian delegation was led by BAI President Mr. Prashant Kumar and President-Elect Mr. Amarjit Singh Chandhiok, along with other office-bearers of the Association.

The discussions focused on strengthening legal cooperation across BRICS+ jurisdictions and exploring areas of mutual engagement, including institutional capacity building, cross-border dispute resolution, legal education and emerging regulatory challenges.

The Forum's programme is structured around economic resilience and the rule of law, climate finance and developmental justice, legal education, arbitration, artificial intelligence governance, digital trust and international investment law.
A 60-member international delegation from the BRICS+ Legal Forum also visited the Supreme Court of India on Friday.
The delegates visited the National Judicial Museum and Archive, the War Room and the Court complex, followed by an interaction with Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant.
The 11th BRICS+ Legal Forum will be inaugurated on August 22 at the India Habitat Centre, with Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant as the Chief Guest.

The inaugural plenary will focus on “Rule of Law in a Multipolar World: Building Legal Capacity for Economic Resilience” and will also feature an address by Attorney General for India Mr. R. Venkataramani.

Hosted by the Bar Association of India, the Forum is being held under the theme “Rule of Law Frameworks and Institutional Capacity Building for Economic Resilience, Innovation and Sustainability.” The programme seeks to move beyond broad dialogue towards practical legal and institutional frameworks for cooperation across BRICS+ jurisdictions.

The substantive programme includes sessions on economic resilience and the rule of law, climate finance and developmental justice, legal education and institutional capacity building, the proposed BRICS Arbitration Network (BRICSAN), AI governance and digital trust, and international investment treaty arbitration.
The closing plenary is scheduled to consider the 11th BRICS+ Legal Forum Declaration, constitute working groups emerging from the deliberations and set the mandate for the 12th Forum.

stories.headline: IMD forecast: Delhi, Noida, Ghaziabad & Gurugram
stories.title: IMD forecast: Delhi, Noida, Ghaziabad & Gurugram
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Residents in the capital region should expect unpredictable weather through the day, with the IMD flagging both rain and thunderstorm activity for the region.
According to the IMD update, Delhi, along with Haryana and Chandigarh, is likely to receive heavy rain at isolated places.

Thunderstorms with lightning and gusty winds are also possible over parts of the Delhi NCR region, making it a good day to carry an umbrella and plan for possible waterlogging or traffic delays in Noida, Gurgaon and Ghaziabad.

Neighbouring Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Uttarakhand are also expected to see heavy rainfall over the weekend, which could have a spillover effect on weather conditions in Delhi NCR in the coming days.

Beyond the Delhi NCR region, the IMD has forecast heavy to very heavy rain in parts of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, the northeastern states, Konkan and Goa, Gujarat, Rajasthan, and parts of south India including Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
Thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds are likely in several of these regions, with rainfall activity expected to remain active nationwide through August 27.

stories.headline: Environment committee discusses conservation, management of J&K lakes
stories.title: Environment committee discusses conservation, management of J&K lakes
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 21: The Committee on Environment on Friday convened for a meeting at Assembly Complex here to discuss and deliberate on measures for the conservation and management of Hokersar, Mansabal, Wular, Nigeen, Mansar and Surinsar Lakes and other wetlands of Jammu and Kashmir. The meeting was chaired by Chairman of the Committee, Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami, and attended by Gharu Ram, Baldev Raj Sharma, Daleep Singh, lShowkat Hussain Ganie, Javaid Ahmad Mirchal, Sajjad Shafi, Rameshwar Singh, and Devyani Rana; members of the committee. The meeting was also attended by Chairman JK PCC Vasu Yadav; CWLW and PCCF WL Suneesh Buxy; VC LCMA, F A LCMA, Regional Wildlife Wardens of Kashmir, Jammu and Rajourivand Poonch, CEO Manasbal Development Authority, Project Coordinator WUCMA, WLWs of Jammu, Wetland and Kathua, and CED WUCMA Wular besides officers of the Assembly Secretariat. Speaking during the meeting, the Chairman stressed that wetlands are vital for ecology, biodiversity and flood mitigation in J&K. He expressed concern over environmental pollution and human interference in these water bodies. He said that everyone has a duty to protect these natural assets for future generations. Reviewing the CAG audit paras, Tarigami said that scientific data and community involvement must guide our conservation efforts. He directed the concerned departments to submit time-bound Action Taken Reports on conservation measures taken for the six major lakes and other wetlands of J&K. The committee was informed that using high-resolution satellite imagery, a comprehensive exercise has been undertaken to identify wetlands across J&K. It was informed that earlier wetlands above 2.25 hectares were mapped, followed by those between 2.25 to 1 hectare, and now even wetlands below 1 hectare are being identified. So far, approximately 1700 wetlands have been identified in J&K. To ensure transparency and easy access, the Department informed that a dedicated State-level portal is being developed having layers for Forest boundaries and Protected Area Network of the Wildlife Department. The Chairman directed that this portal be made public-friendly. He said that the portal will help clear confusion about boundaries and will be accessible to members, departments, and the public. The Chairman directed that the portal should include data on vegetation, water bodies, rivers and other ecological features in a phased manner. He emphasised that public access to this data will bring greater accountability and community participation in wetland conservation.
